Maladaptive Strategies.value: I keep asking others to reassure me that I am okay
always plan an escape route before entering a place

Threat.value: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel
My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard

issues.item: Compulsive Cleaning: I clean or organise things repeatedly to feel in control
issues.explanation: Compulsive cleaning is not well supported by the rest of the profile. The threat items describe hypervigilance and safety-positioning in response to interpersonal danger, but no other item suggests contamination, orderliness, or a ritualised control theme. As a maladaptive strategy, it feels disconnected from the threat pattern represented here.

issues.item: Memory Detachment: I detach myself from the memories
issues.explanation: The formulation has Threat strongly linked with Maladaptive Strategies, while Memory is isolated with no active edges. The maladaptive strategy items should therefore be tightly connected to current threat management. 'Memory Detachment' is a memory-focused coping response that implies an active Memory-related process, which is not reflected elsewhere and does not align with the specified edge pattern. In contrast, reassurance seeking, hypervigilance towards people, and the threat items form a coherent threat-management cluster for captivity trauma.

vignette:
Tama is a 53-year-old photographer who, three years ago, was sent to cover a political uprising in a small Pacific island nation. While driving between villages, his vehicle was stopped by armed militia. They blindfolded him, bound his hands, and held him for seventeen days in a concrete room. He never saw his captors' faces, but he learned to read their moods through the pitch of their voices, the speed of their footsteps, the way the door would slam or creak open. He was certain at any moment they would kill him. When he finally escaped during a chaotic firefight, he ran for hours through the jungle, not stopping until he reached a coastal town.

Back home in Honolulu, Tama tried to resume his life as a wedding and event photographer. But the world felt different. Every venue he entered for a shoot, he would first scan for exits-where the back door was, whether a window could open, whether a hallway led to a dead end. He always chose a spot to stand that gave him a clear view of the room and kept his back to a wall. If a guest moved suddenly toward him-raising a hand to wave, stepping quickly to catch a falling champagne flute-Tama's chest would seize, his muscles would harden, and for a split second he would forget he was holding a camera, not running for his life. His body was constantly tense, coiled like an animal that had learned never to relax. He began to ask his wife, Maya, every morning: "Do I look okay? Are we safe? Is this normal?" He would text her multiple times during a job just to hear her say everything was fine.

The more he watched for danger, the more danger he found. A man standing too still near the bar. A woman laughing too loudly. The way a door swung shut. Each time his body went on alert, Tama felt a fresh wave of certainty that danger was real-and then he would check the exits again, shift his position, text Maya for reassurance. The reassurance worked for a few minutes, then the doubt crept back. He had come to believe that his safety depended on never letting his guard down, that if he stopped monitoring the room, something terrible would happen. But the monitoring itself exhausted him. At the last wedding he photographed, he spent so much time planning escape routes and watching guests' movements that he missed the couple's first kiss. The bride's mother complained. Maya, after months of comforting him, finally said she couldn't keep telling him he was safe when he never seemed to believe her.

That was what brought Tama to seek help. He was afraid of losing his wife, afraid of losing his career, but most of all afraid that the captivity had changed something permanent in him-that he would spend the rest of his life watching shadows, never able to lower his shoulders or trust that the door would stay closed. He hoped, quietly, that a therapist could teach him how to unlearn the vigilance that had kept him alive in that room, but was now keeping him from living.
